questions.q: During starvation or extreme low-carbohydrate intake, the body breaks down muscle protein to synthesize glucose for the brain. What is this process called?
questions.explain: Gluconeogenesis is the metabolic pathway that results in the generation of glucose from non-carbohydrate carbon substrates, such as glucogenic amino acids from muscle protein.

questions.q: What happens to the structure of a protein when it is exposed to the hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
options: It is denatured, uncoiling the polypeptide chain.
It forms a double helix structure.
questions.explain: HCl in the stomach denatures proteins, meaning it disrupts their secondary and tertiary structures (uncoiling them), making the peptide bonds more accessible to enzymatic action by pepsin.

questions.q: A 'Complete Protein' is defined as a protein source that:
options: Contains all 20 amino acids in equal amounts.
Is derived exclusively from animal sources.
Contains all 9 essential amino acids in adequate proportions.
Has a high ratio of unsaturated fats to protein.
questions.explain: High-quality or 'complete' proteins contain all 9 essential amino acids in the amounts needed to support protein synthesis in the body. Most animal proteins and soy are complete.

questions.q: Edema (swelling) is a clinical sign of severe protein deficiency (Kwashiorkor). This occurs because:
options: Albumin levels drop, reducing oncotic pressure and allowing fluid to leak into interstitial spaces.
Excess protein causes water retention in the kidneys.
The body is burning too much fat, producing metabolic water.
questions.explain: Proteins like albumin maintain oncotic pressure (fluid balance) in the blood. A deficiency leads to fluid leaking from blood vessels into tissues, causing edema.
